title: Thyroid Storm: A Multi-Drug Approach

items.text: A life-threatening hyperthyroid crisis requiring rapid, multi-pronged therapy.

emphasis.text: A life-threatening hyperthyroid crisis requiring rapid, multi-pronged therapy.

items.text: Beta-blockers (propranolol) — control adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) and also blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.
items.md: Beta-blockers (propranolol) — control adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) and also blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.

items.text: Corticosteroids — also blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency.
items.md: Corticosteroids — also blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency.

The "iodine after PTU, not before" sequencing is a classic high-yield detail — giving iodine first can actually worsen the crisis by providing more substrate for hormone synthesis before synthesis is blocked.

notes:
Supporting drugs at a glance. Antipsychotics and metoclopramide — Raise prolactin by blocking dopamine. Calcium, iron and antacids — Block levothyroxine absorption; separate by 4 hours. Amiodarone and lithium — Can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism. Estrogens — Raise thyroid-binding globulin, so levothyroxine needs rise. Rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine — Speed clearance of levothyroxine and steroids. Azole antifungals — Raise corticosteroid exposure through CYP3A4. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium — Add to spironolactone hyperkalemia. Insulin and oral agents — Doses need adjusting during steroid therapy. Listed for context; not profiled in detail.
